President Bola Tinubu risked his life and political future by returning to Nigeria shortly after the death of military dictator, General Sani Abacha, in 1998, overruling the caution of fellow pro-democracy exiles just to see his mother. The disclosure is contained in Chapter 11, pages 185–187, of ‘From AD to APC: The Evolution of Nigerian Political Parties and the Exploits of One Man (1998–2015),’ a new book by veteran journalist Sam Omatseye. The excerpt was included in the programme of events for the book’s public presentation on Tuesday at the State House Conference Centre, Abuja, which was to be attended by the President. According to the book, Tinubu, who was in exile, expressed a desire to see his mother during an emergency meeting in London convened by NADECO Abroad following Abacha’s sudden death in June 1998. “It was in a room in London, and members of the NADECO Abroad had convened. “The meeting was tense. An earthquake had happened at home, and the consequence was one for the ages. The dictator Sani Abacha had died,” the excerpt read. According to Omatseye, although the new military Head of State, General Abdulsalami Abubakar, had conveyed a conciliatory tone to civil society organisations, suspicions ran deep. Those present at the London meeting included former Foreign Affairs Minister, Professor Bolaji Akinyemi; retired General Alani Akinrinade; and Prince Iludoyin, all of whom had endured exile and deprivation, with the constant fear of being captured by the regime. He wrote, “Most did not want to return just yet. They still wanted to watch the direction of affairs. There was a sense in which caution made sense. “The military from the times of Babangida had laid ambush against the political society.” Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. He warned that a delay would hand the political space to those who had propped up military rule. “If they delayed and stayed back, they would surrender the country to the apologists of the military. “They were the members of the five leprous fingers, and they could execute a pirouette and style themselves as democrats. “It would turn the work of all of them, who had lost lives and resources, into a waste. He did not want that,” it read. Omatseye added, “Tinubu tried to persuade them to take the plunge, and that the death of Abacha meant the decapitation of an era.” Nonetheless, his fellow exiles hesitated, arguing that it made sense to visit Nigeria first and assess the situation rather than commit to a full return. Tinubu said in 1992 he wanted to govern Nigeria — Olanipekun Summon parties over violence, Dickson urges Abdulsalami panel, INEC Amupitan and the ghosts of November Addressing his reluctant comrades, Tinubu revealed that his real reason for returning to the country was to see his mother again, Omatseye wrote. “So, in order to provide an excuse, he brought in a sense of domestic humour to disarm his fellows. He burst out in Yoruba, ‘Mo fe lo ri maami.’ (I want to see my mother.) They were amused but they had no counterpoint to his cheerful alibi,” the book stated. The 1998 meeting followed the death of Abacha, who seized power from the Ernest Shonekan-led Interim National Government several months after the annulment of the June 12, 1993, presidential election won by Chief MKO Abiola. Abiola died in custody on July 7, 1998. General Abdulsalami subsequently oversaw a transition programme that produced the 1999 Constitution and transferred power to civilian rule on May 29, 1999. Tinubu, a former senator who contested the 1992 senatorial election on the Social Democratic Party platform, returned from exile and contested the Lagos governorship election under the Alliance for Democracy, winning in 1999 and beginning the political journey that would eventually take him to the presidency in 2023. The book, which covers the period from 1998 to 2015, tracing Nigeria’s return to civilian rule through the collapse of the Peoples Democratic Party’s 16-year grip on federal power, is Omatseye’s second major political work. His first, ‘Beating All Odds: How Bola Tinubu Became President,’ was published in 2024. An award-winning journalist, author, poet and playwright, Omatseye is Chairman of the Editorial Board of The Nation newspaper, where his weekly column, In Touch, has run for two decades. Born on June 15, 1961, he studied History at the University of Ife, now Obafemi Awolowo University, and began his career at Newswatch magazine before rising to deputy political editor at Concord Newspapers during the June 12 crisis. He was beaten by soldiers while covering the 1992 Ejigbo air crash. He later won the Nigerian Media Merit Award for Reporter of the Year. Omatseye has won three additional NMMAs as Columnist of the Year and four Diamond Awards for Media Excellence. He is also a recipient of the Association of Black Journalists’ Features Prize and the Scripps Howard Award for deadline reporting. He was the inaugural recipient of the Gordon N. Fisher Commonwealth Fellowship for Journalists. He was among 51 persons granted national honours by the President in his 2026 Democracy Day speech on June 12. According to the programme of events, the gathering was scheduled to receive goodwill messages from the governors of Lagos, Delta and Kaduna states, as well as former Zamfara Governor Abdulaziz Yari, former APC National Chairman Adams Oshiomhole, Minister of Environment Tunji Bello, media executive Dapo Olorunyomi and Alex Kabba. The book was scheduled to be reviewed by Louis Odion, with excerpts to be read by Ohi Alegbe, Stella Din Jacobs and Yomi Odunuga. Stephen Angbulu With three years of experience, Stephen, The PUNCH correspondent, has been covering Nigeria’s presidency, politics, security, immigration and trafficking in persons
